title: Cossack Mamay
summary: Cossack Mamay, or Kozak Mamai, is a prominent folklore hero in Ukraine, symbolizing the spirit and culture of the [[cossacks|Cossacks]]. His image has been widely represented in various forms of Ukrainian art and literature, especially following the dissolution of the Zaporozhian Sich in 1775.

sections.heading: Historical Overview
paragraphs: Cossack Mamay appears in numerous legends, folk stories, and proverbs, gaining popularity particularly after the dissolution of the [[zaporizhian-sich|Zaporozhian Sich]] in 1775. He is a central figure in [[ukrainian|Ukrainian]] folk painting from the late 17th century to the present, often depicted with a kobza, a horse, and an oak tree with weapons, symbolizing freedom, fidelity, and strength.

sections.heading: Artistic Representation
paragraphs: Cossack Mamay is a common subject in traditional folk paintings, characterized by the figure of a Cossack sitting with crossed legs. Various paintings, known as 'Cossack-Bandurist,' 'Cossack-Zaporozhets,' and 'Cossack Mamai,' share similar compositional features and have existed for centuries in Ukrainian culture. Major collections of these artworks are housed in the National Art Museum of [[ukraine|Ukraine]], the [[dnieper|Dnipro]] Historical Museum named after Dmytro Yavornytskyi, and the Ivan Honchar Museum.

sections.heading: Cossack Mamay in Literature and Film
paragraphs: The character of Cossack Mamay has inspired several literary works, including the novel 'No End to Cossack Kin' by Olexandr Ilchenko, the historical verse novel 'Mamay' by Leonid Gorlach, and the poetry collection 'The Cossack Mamay Myth' by Ihor Kalynets. In film, the 2003 movie 'Mamay,' directed by Oles Sanin, further explores this iconic figure.

sections.heading: Musical and Street Art Representations
paragraphs: Cossack Mamay's image has also been reflected in contemporary [[music-of-ukraine|Ukrainian music]], with songs by bands such as Komu Vnyz and Vopli Vidoplyasova. During the [[revolution-of-dignity|Revolution of Dignity]], artist Mykola Goncharov reinterpreted Cossack Mamay in street art, creating graffiti and posters that modernized his image by incorporating contemporary symbols.

sections.heading: Cossack Mamay Coin
paragraphs: In 1997, the [[national-bank-of-ukraine|National Bank of Ukraine]] minted a coin featuring Cossack Mamay, depicting him in a rich coat, smoking a pipe, and playing a kobza. The coin includes traditional elements of Cossack life, such as a horse, a green oak tree, and various weapons. The inscriptions on the coin highlight his identity as 'Cossack Mamay' and 'Knight of Freedom and Honor,' reflecting his significance in Ukrainian heritage.
